item.title: Turning Implications Into Evidence: Actionable Solutions to Real-World Problems of Practice and Policy Based on Prior Academy of Management Publications
item.content:encoded:
Julian Birkinshaw, Western University

Thomas P. Lyon, University of Michigan

Denise M. Rousseau, Carnegie Mellon University

Majken Schultz, Copenhagen Business School

Mo Wang, University of Florida

Amid rising concern about the relevance of their contents, many scholarly journals mandate inclusion of a managerial implications section. This section may be relegated to a few paragraphs at the end of an article and comprised of speculative statements loosely connected to the paper's empirical or theoretical content. And there these unvalidated implications tend to remain, largely unaddressed in future research studies and having little relevance to practice or policy.

This special issue calls for original research that develops actionable solutions from previously published managerial implications. By developing actionable insights from underdeveloped or dormant implications, this special issue furthers the core function of any science: the development of a corpus of valid and reliable knowledge. An applied science has the added demand that knowledge be usable outside of academia.

The portfolio of Academy of Management journals forms a system of knowledge production in which each journal has a complementary specialization. Within this system, Academy of Management Perspectives papers provide actionable insights that guide practitioner behavior and influence policy decisions. These papers build on theory developed, tested, and organized in other journals and enrich these theories by revealing nuances and boundaries of their usefulness.

This special issue is limited to papers that analyze practice and policy implications previously published in any of the seven established Academy of Management journals: Academy of Management Annals, Academy of Management Collections, Academy of Management Discoveries, Academy of Management Journal, Academy of Management Learning & Education, Academy of Management Review, and Academy of Management Perspectives. The article containing the focal implication on which a submission is based must have been published in or fully accepted to any of these journals at any point up to 31 December 2026.

Submissions must conduct novel empirical or conceptual analysis. Academy of Management Perspectives does not accept managerial translations that restate previously published work in more practice-friendly terms. Moreover, papers that address managerial implications for which actionable solutions have already been adequately developed through prior publications are not accepted. Authors submitting to this special issue may be, but are not required to be, an author of the published article containing the managerial implication.

Academy of Management Perspectives' mission and format differ from many other leading academic journals. Though the format differs, the journal's analytical standards are the same as at any other Academy of Management journal, demanding robust analysis that fulfills current social science standards. Papers should be grounded in evidence or robust conceptual frameworks, address relevant real-world managerial and policy issues, offer actionable insights, avoid theory fetish, and be written in a style accessible to non-specialists and practitioners.

A Paper Development Workshop will be hosted at the Academy of Management 2026 Conference in Philadelphia for selected authors to further develop their manuscripts. Participation in this workshop is neither a guarantee nor a prerequisite for publication.

Potential topics

  • Developing actionable solutions from previously published managerial implications
  • Novel empirical or conceptual analysis of practice and policy implications
  • Real-world problems of practice and policy overlooked in managerial implications sections
  • Robust analysis providing specific guidance for practitioners and policy makers
  • Building on theory developed in Academy of Management journals to enrich and reveal nuances of their usefulness

Timeline

  • January 1, 2026: Call for papers opens
  • January 31, 2027: Submission deadline at 23:59 ET

Associate editors

  • Michael L. Barnett, Rutgers University

item.title: Managing Under Political Turbulence
item.content:encoded:
Jonathan Doh, Villanova University

Srividya Jandhyala, ESSEC Business School

Yadong Luo, University of Miami

Grazia D. Santangelo, Copenhagen Business School

Political turbulence is on the rise, as evidenced most dramatically in violent conflicts (e.g., wars, terrorism attacks), volatile political transitions (e.g., dramatic regime change, cuts to government employees, new geopolitical alliances, coups), and geopolitical tensions (e.g., trade wars, democratic backsliding, sanctions). This escalated political turbulence exacerbates geopolitical risks for organizations and their stakeholders.

Whether anticipatory (e.g., fear of cyberattacks) or actual (e.g., ongoing trade wars, competition over territories), rising geopolitical risks affect organizations in many ways. The rise of techno-nationalism, driven by national security and ideological concerns, challenges the resilience of global technology supply chains. With the rapid development of AI comes misinformation and disinformation that further aggravate political tensions and ideologies. Tariffs, sanctions, and protectionist trade restrictions bring escalating compliance risks. Rising populist sentiment drives immigration restrictions and is creating a shortage of high-skill talent for MNEs.

Political turbulence has long been a strategic consideration in some sectors such as energy and defense, but it is now affecting organizations in nearly all sectors, both at home and abroad. At home, organizations encounter scrutiny from civil society for their operations in countries with questionable international standing. Abroad, they may face interventions by host country governments that vary with their country of origin or type of ownership. All of this presents considerable challenges for managers and their organizations.

This special issue aims to provide actionable, evidence-based insights that clearly and credibly guide managers and their organizations in navigating the political turbulence that increasingly characterizes the international, national, and subnational landscape. We seek to fill in the 'glaring white space' of how organizations can best operate under political turbulence, providing robust insights on which practitioners and policy makers can rely.

AMP papers are managerially driven, not theory driven. Successful submissions clearly define the managerial issue from the outset and make a compelling case for its importance. They do not simply tack managerial implications onto a standard academic study. Rather, AMP papers evidence actionable insights that can credibly guide managerial behavior and influence policy decisions.

We welcome both conceptual and empirical papers that are grounded in rigorous analysis and directly evidence specific and significant managerial and policy actions. We welcome accounts of embodied, lived experiences of specific political turbulence and the use of reflexive methodologies. Quantitative analyses of large databases, qualitative comparative analyses, and extensive data analysis using linguistic programs and algorithms are also welcome. Papers should prove what can or does work in ways that managers and policymakers can use.

Potential topics

  • Understanding Different Types and Forms of Political Turbulence
  • Rethinking Corporate Political Strategies
  • Reorganizing and Realigning Geographically Diversified Operations
  • Managing Stakeholder Nationalism
  • The Role of New Technologies
  • Managing Corporate Innovation
  • Navigating the Race for Talent

Timeline

  • September 1, 2026: Submission window opens
  • September 30, 2026: Final deadline for submissions at 23:59 ET

Associate editors

  • Tazeeb Rajwani, University of Surrey

item.title: Open Call for Papers
item.content:encoded:
Academy of Management Perspectives (AMP) publishes papers that matter to managers. The journal seeks to realize the field's long-standing call for managerially relevant work. AMP papers must be managerially driven from the start, not theory-driven papers with managerial implications added as an afterthought. Papers rejected from theory-focused journals are not suitable for AMP unless they are fundamentally reoriented toward managerial relevance.

AMP papers must meet three core criteria: they must be RELEVANT, RIGOROUS, and READABLE. Relevant papers inform an issue of evident importance to managerial practice and/or policy. Rigorous papers engage in rigorous and original conceptual or empirical analysis. Readable papers concisely and clearly convey key ideas to a non-specialized audience. All three criteria must be satisfied.

While managerial relevance is the journal's most prominent characteristic, it does not come at the expense of rigor. AMP does not publish papers lacking rigorous original analysis. The analytical standards are the same as those of other elite journals. Opinions, overviews, descriptive arguments, and philosophical treatises are not within the journal's purview, even if they convey interesting perspectives on management. The managers who rely on AMP content need evidence, not conjecture.

AMP manuscripts differ in format from other Academy of Management journals to enhance accessibility for non-specialized audiences. The journal uses endnotes, places detailed analyses in supplements, and limits body pages to approximately 20 pages rather than the standard 30+. AMP papers favor plain language over jargon and make the practical case from the start rather than appending managerial implications at the end.

A typical AMP manuscript includes the following components: an engaging title and concise abstract of no more than 200 words; a concise introduction serving as an executive summary; a problem statement that clearly articulates the focal managerial issue and makes a convincing case for its importance; a review of relevant literature portraying baseline knowledge; identification of gaps in current understanding; rigorous conceptual or empirical analysis providing evidence to address the identified gaps; discussion of what has been learned including implementation steps and boundary conditions; and a brief conclusion restating the paper's contributions and significance.

Potential topics

  • Papers that inform managerial practice and policy
  • Work addressing issues of evident importance to managerial practice and/or policy
  • Rigorous and original conceptual or empirical analysis
  • Papers accessible to non-specialized audiences and practitioners
  • Work grounded in evidence or robust conceptual frameworks
  • Papers offering actionable insights for managers and policymakers

Timeline

  • January 31, 2027: Submission deadline
